items.passage: "Mind the corner; it has gone slack," Ingeborg said, before she had even removed her gloves. We had not spoken in eleven years. The banner lay where I had unrolled it across the floor of the school gymnasium, between the vaulting horse and the ropes, its border of Rotterdam's bridges half stitched. Our mother had begun it for the school's jubilee; we had quarrelled over the colour of the river and left it in a trunk. I offered Ingeborg the stool, as one offers a visitor. She took the floor instead, kneeling where she had always knelt, on the left. We worked until the lamps were lit, speaking only of thread prices and the caretaker's cough. Once she reached for the grey silk, paused, and took the blue. I said nothing. When the caretaker came to lock the doors, she rolled up her half of the banner with mine inside it, the way our mother used to, so that neither end would crease.

items.passage: When I was sixteen, my violin lessons took place in the back room of a seed-saving cooperative in Tromso, between shelves of labeled envelopes: dwarf peas, northern kale, a barley nobody had planted since 1950. Anders, my teacher, sorted seeds while I played and corrected my bowing without looking up. In March he informed me that he had entered me in the conservatory audition in Oslo, with a sonata he had picked out himself. He had not asked. I said thank you in the tone one uses for a parking ticket. For three months I practiced the sonata in that room, and he sorted seeds, and neither of us mentioned the entry form. The night before I left, I found a paper envelope in my violin case, labeled in his square handwriting: barley, 1950, keep dry. I have it still. I have not planted it, and I have not thrown it away.

items.passage: Chalk dust covered my sleeves by the time the evening class ended at the language school on Hang Bai Street. Lan stayed behind, as she had every Tuesday since she moved back to Hanoi, and addressed me as Teacher Anh, the way the other students did. I called her Miss Lan and corrected her English verbs. My younger brother, who was nine, still asked why she had stopped coming to our house after her family left for Da Nang. I had told him she was busy. That Tuesday Lan handed me an envelope: the tuition I had waived for her in September, counted out in small notes. I pushed it back across the desk. She left it on my brother's school notebook, which I had been marking during the break. Before she went, she copied a sentence into its margin in careful English, I am sorry I did not say goodbye, and drew a small bicycle beside it, the kind we used to ride along the lake.

items.passage: When the last crate of my father's records was sold, Ofelia counted the bills twice on the folding table between the lemons and the fish stalls of the Valparaiso market. I had called her Señora all morning, the way I called the woman who ran the bakery, and she answered to it without correcting me. The plan had been hers: sell the records before the rent came due, keep the apartment, keep me at the same school. It had worked. A man in a striped scarf carried off the jazz albums, and a student took the rest in two trips. Ofelia divided the bills into two stacks, slid the thicker one toward me, and said, Count it, Emiliano. She folded the thinner one into her apron. Then, while I was watching the gulls over the harbor, she took the thinner stack out again, set it on top of mine, and smoothed the empty apron pocket flat. Neither of us mentioned it. On the walk uphill she carried the empty crates.

items.passage: Who keeps a radio playing through a wall for eleven years without once asking whether anyone minds? I did, on the old barge moored below the Busan fish wharf, where my cabin and Bokhee's share a single plank partition and my name, Eunseo, is painted on the door in white. I have always called her Mrs. Bokhee and bowed at the gangway, and she has always bowed back, a little lower. Each New Year she left a jar of pickled radish outside my door; I left nothing, assuming the radish was simply what neighbors on the river did. This spring I switched the radio off at nine and kept it off. On the third quiet night I heard her drag something heavy across her floor. In the morning, through her open door, I saw her narrow bed pushed back against our shared wall, its old place by the drafty window now empty, a square of unfaded boards showing where it had stood for years. I bought radish seeds that afternoon.

items.passage: Rattle of window glass, smell of diesel and orange peel: Aigerim had graded on this line out of Cairo for nine years, a red pencil behind her ear. Somewhere past Giza she took it down and began on the stack in her lap, circling, striking, writing a small hard number at the top of each page. When the door slid open, Yusuf stood there with a ticket for the same compartment. He had been her student four years earlier; she had once written a single red word across his final essay, and he had left the course the next week. He sat across from her. Neither spoke. She went on grading, and now the pencil hovered above each margin before it touched, and twice she lifted it without making a mark. Yusuf took a notebook from his bag and wrote, page after page. Near Minya he stood to leave. Aigerim turned the pencil around and held it out to him, blunt end first. He looked at it, then took it.

items.passage: Four rules held in the tailor's back room, which Weiqi and I rented on alternating mornings in that Vermont winter to proof our dough: no talk of prices, no borrowing flour, no opening the window, and nothing of mine crosses the chalk line on the floor. I had drawn that line myself, heel to heel across the boards, and each Monday I traced it again so it would not wear away. Weiqi, whose bakery stood three doors from mine, kept to her side without comment. On Thursday a letter arrived with the tailor's name on it, and Weiqi, thinking it was for her, had opened it before she noticed. It was from the landlord: the building would be sold in spring. She read it aloud to me anyway, standing on her side. We stood a long while among the rising bowls. When she left, I stepped forward, and my boot rested on the chalk. My name is Matheus, and I did not retrace it that Monday, or the next.

items.passage: Polishing the brass bell was the first chore Kai ever gave Tallulah, in 1921, after the galley of a scrapped steamer was hauled by rail to Albuquerque and bolted down as a lunch counter on Central Avenue. Kai rang it for every order, two strokes for coffee, three for stew, and the railroad men learned the code before they learned the menu. The counter had come to the two of them jointly from Kai's brother, and by the fourth summer Tallulah wanted to sell her half and ride west. Kai heard her out over the evening dishes. For a week after, orders went up by voice alone; the bell hung dull and silent, and no one touched the rag folded beside it. On the last night of that week, Kai lifted the bell from its hook, rubbed it once with his sleeve, and set it on Tallulah's packed trunk by the door.

items.passage: When the power failed across Old Dhaka, the night pharmacy where Tara worked became the only lit room on the lane, and by midnight two families had brought their festival trays to its single steel table. Tara's aunt set down rice pudding for Eid. Hari, who had sailed cargo ships for thirty years and now lived above the shop, arrived with a brass plate of marigolds and sweets for his evening prayer. Three times he set the plate down near the corner, and three times he drew it back toward his chest when someone reached past him. Hari's plate rode at the table's rim, an anchored skiff off a crowded quay. Tara shifted the pudding bowls to open a gap. He looked at the gap and kept still, holding the plate level. Only when her aunt tapped the empty steel twice with one finger did he slide the marigolds into the middle, and the flame of his small lamp leaned toward the rice.

is drawing on long habits formed during his years on cargo ships.

items.passage: Years later I still picture Angus at the crossing below Kelvin Mill, where the burn had dried that August to a bed of grey stones. I was nineteen and clerked for him three mornings a week, long after he had left the bench; he called me Miss Maeve and never anything shorter. Every morning he carried an envelope addressed in his own hand to a man he had once sentenced, and every morning, at the near edge of the stones, he pressed two fingers flat against the pocket that held it. For him that envelope was a ford walked daily toward a bank that never came nearer. I would wait with the satchel while he stood there. On the last dry morning, with not a trickle left between the stones, he stepped out to the middle, stood beside a flat rock as long as it takes to read a page, and walked back to me. We went round by the bridge.

an obstacle that conditions outside Angus keep firmly in his way.
a duty from his years on the bench that still shapes his days.

items.passage:
Smell of split guava, sweet and gone to vinegar,
the wasps loud in it. Ximena signed the deed in March
and paid the last wage in an envelope with the gate code inside.
Still, each dawn, Kiara walks the rows above Kingston
lifting what the wind brought down,
